title: 2 Thessalonians
subtitle: Not yet: hold your ground, and keep working
lead: A short letter to a young church under pressure. The believers at Thessalonica, mostly Gentile converts in the chief city of Roman Macedonia, were being persecuted by their neighbors, and someone had told them, by a prophecy, a teaching or a letter claiming to be from Paul, that "the day of the Lord is already here". Some members had stopped working and were living off the others.

The letter answers all three. It promises that God sees their suffering and will do justice when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven (chapter 1). It insists that the day has not come, because the rebellion and "the man of lawlessness" must come first, though something is holding him back for now (chapter 2). And it commands the church to keep apart from those who will not work, while still treating them as brothers (chapter 3). Its few verses on the man of lawlessness and the one who holds him back have produced more speculation than almost any other passage in Paul, and the question of who wrote the letter divides scholars: a 2011 survey at one British conference found a majority for Paul, with many unsure, while others, following Trilling and Menken, hold that a follower wrote it.
facts: Traditionally Paul, with Silvanus and Timothy (1:1; 3:17). Scholars are divided: many hold that Paul wrote it soon after 1 Thessalonians; many others that a follower wrote it in his name decades later. See the authorship table.

If Paul wrote it, about AD 51-52, from Corinth, a few weeks or months after 1 Thessalonians (a few scholars, among them Wanamaker, put it before 1 Thessalonians). If a follower wrote it, about AD 80-115.
If Paul wrote it, probably Corinth, where Paul, Silas and Timothy were together (Acts 18:5). The KJV's closing note, 'written from Athens', is a later scribe's guess.
The church at Thessalonica, founded by Paul, Silas and Timothy (Acts 17:1-9): mostly Gentile converts from the worship of idols (1 Thessalonians 1:9), with some Jews and God-fearers.

A letter, with a thanksgiving that becomes a vision of judgment (chapter 1), a short apocalyptic teaching (2:1-12), a thanksgiving and call to stand firm (2:13-17), and commands about church order (chapter 3), closed in Paul's own hand.
Greek, close in wording to 1 Thessalonians, with many phrases from the Greek Old Testament (Isaiah, Daniel, Psalms).
authorship: It names Paul, Silvanus and Timothy (1:1), speaks in Paul's own voice ("I kept telling you this", 2:5), and ends: "The greeting is in my own hand, Paul's. That is the sign in every letter" (3:17).

The church received it as Paul's from the second century, and many scholars still do. A survey at the British New Testament Conference in 2011 found 63 of 111 scholars for Paul, 13 against and 35 unsure. Abraham Malherbe (Anchor Bible, 2000) gives a full case for Paul and answers Trilling's arguments; Charles Wanamaker (1990) defends Paul and argues that this letter was actually written first. Others who hold to Paul include Leon Morris, Gene Green, G. K. Beale, Ben Witherington III and N. T. Wright. Their arguments: the letter answers a real crisis in the same church weeks later, so the repetition of 1 Thessalonians is natural; apocalyptic writing combines signs and suddenness, as Jesus' sayings do; and the worry about a forged letter (2:2) explains the stress on the signature (3:17).

Since J. E. C. Schmidt (1798) and William Wrede (1903), many scholars have held that a follower of Paul wrote it. Wolfgang Trilling's study (1972) changed many minds in Germany, and Maarten Menken (1994) and Eduard Verhoef (1997) argue the same; others who doubt Paul include Bart Ehrman, Beverly Gaventa, Udo Schnelle and Eugene Boring. Their arguments: the letter copies the structure and phrases of 1 Thessalonians too closely for a letter written soon after it, yet its tone is cooler; its timetable of signs (2:3-12) conflicts with the sudden coming of the thief in 1 Thessalonians 5:2; it refers to letters of Paul (2:2, 15; 3:17) in a way that suits a time when they were collected; and 'the sign in every letter' reads like a forger's guarantee.

Some reverse the order of the two letters, so that this one came first (Wanamaker). Among those who think a follower wrote it, the letter's relation to 1 Thessalonians is itself debated: whether it was meant to stand beside the first letter or to correct the way it was being read.

The Plain English Translation follows the text and calls the writer Paul, as the letter does. The notes give both views where they matter (1:1, 1:3, 2:2, 2:15, 3:17), and the chapter pages set out the arguments under the Critical lens.

audience.to: The church at Thessalonica, the chief city and capital of the Roman province of Macedonia, on the main road from Italy to the East. Paul, Silas and Timothy had founded it a short time before, in a stay cut short by a riot (Acts 17:1-10). Its members were mostly Gentiles who had turned away from idols to God (1 Thessalonians 1:9), with some Jews and God-fearing Greeks and "many women of the first rank" (Acts 17:4); most worked with their hands (1 Thessalonians 4:11). They had received 1 Thessalonians, and were still being persecuted by their neighbors (1:4). If the letter is by a later follower, the readers are Paul's churches a generation on, for whom Thessalonica stands as an example.
audience.why: Three problems: persecution that made the believers wonder whether God was with them; a claim, said to come from Paul, that the day of the Lord had already arrived, which unsettled them; and members who had stopped working and were living on others. The letter answers with a promise of God's justice (chapter 1), a reminder of what must come first (chapter 2) and a command to restore order (chapter 3). Knowing the audience changes the reading: the judgment of chapter 1 is comfort for the powerless, not a threat to outsiders; the strange details of chapter 2 were enough for readers who had already heard Paul's teaching (2:5) and are dark only to us; and the rule of 3:10 was given to a small church, about its own members who shared its food.
views: The same church, the same crisis, a second letter from Corinth soon after the first: the persecution has grown and a false claim about the day has arisen (Malherbe; Wanamaker, who puts this letter first).
A follower writes to a later generation
Decades later, a follower of Paul uses his name and his first letter to speak to Paul's churches, most likely to cool end-time excitement. Trilling and Menken argue for a later writer.

outline: Greeting from Paul, Silvanus and Timothy
Thanks for faith and love that grow under persecution
God's just judgment: rest for the troubled when the Lord Jesus is revealed
A prayer that God will make them worthy
Do not be shaken: the day of the Lord is not here
What must come first: the rebellion, the man of lawlessness, the one holding him back, and his defeat
Chosen and called: hold the traditions
A prayer for comfort and strength
Pray for us; the Lord is faithful
Members who live out of line: work quietly, keep apart, but treat them as brothers
Peace, Paul's own signature, and grace

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads the letter against Thessalonica, the chief city of Roman Macedonia: the church's founding in conflict (Acts 17), persecution by neighbors, patrons and clients, manual workers, the memory of Antiochus IV and of Caligula's attempt to put his statue in the Temple in AD 40.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks who wrote the letter and when: Paul soon after 1 Thessalonians (Malherbe, Wanamaker) or a follower decades later (Wrede, Trilling, Menken); the close literary relation to 1 Thessalonians; the differences in its view of the end; the letter's own words about forged letters and Paul's signature; and the text's variants.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Reads the shape of the letter: the long sentence of thanksgiving and judgment (1:3-10), the apocalyptic pattern of 2:1-12 with the lawless one as a dark mirror of Christ, the answering thanksgiving (2:13-15), the prayers that close each section, and the word play on work and order in chapter 3.

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Traces the letter's language to the Scriptures of Israel and Jewish apocalyptic hope: Isaiah 2, 11 and 66, Daniel 7-12 and the arrogant king, Ezekiel 28, the Psalms, the vindication of the persecuted faithful; and notes how texts about Israel's God are applied to Jesus.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: Follows how the churches have read the letter: the fathers on the Antichrist and the restrainer (Irenaeus, Tertullian, Chrysostom, Augustine), the Reformers' identification of the papacy, dispensational readings of the restrainer and the rapture, the debate over tradition at 2:15, teachings on hell (1:9), and practices of church discipline (3:14-15).

sections.b:
Read it with 1 Thessalonians open beside it. The two letters share senders, readers, many phrases and the same two concerns: the Lord's coming and the order of the church's life. Where 1 Thessalonians says the day will come suddenly, as a thief comes (1 Thessalonians 5:2), this letter says it has not come yet and lists what must happen first. Where 1 Thessalonians gently urged the idle to work (4:11-12; 5:14), this letter commands it.

Read chapter 2 slowly and humbly. Paul writes to people who had heard his fuller teaching in person (2:5), so he speaks in hints: "You know, too, what is holding him back" (2:6). Later readers, from Augustine on, have admitted that they do not know. The notes give the main readings without choosing among them where the text does not decide. Key words keep the same English throughout: coming (parousia), appearing (epiphaneia), revealing (apokalypsis), the rebellion, the man of lawlessness, the son of ruin, what is holding him back, out of line (ataktos), traditions.

Each chapter ends with a prayer or blessing (1:11-12; 2:16-17; 3:16). Chapter 1 is a thanksgiving that becomes a vision of judgment, all one sentence in Greek (1:3-10). Chapter 2 is the heart: a correction of the claim that the day has come (2:1-12), built as a short apocalypse, and a thanksgiving that sets the readers on the side of truth (2:13-17). Chapter 3 turns to practice: prayer, then the long command about the idle (3:6-15), then the signature.

A pattern of mirrors runs through chapter 2. The lawless one has his own "coming" (2:9) and "revealing" (2:3, 6, 8), his own signs and wonders, his own believers who believe "the lie". Against him stands the Lord Jesus, whose coming and appearing undo him with a breath (2:8).

The two letters open almost identically (1:1-2 and 1 Thessalonians 1:1), give thanks in the same words (1:3 and 1 Thessalonians 1:2-3; 2:13 and 1 Thessalonians 2:13), describe Paul's work night and day in nearly the same sentence (3:8 and 1 Thessalonians 2:9), and close with the same kind of blessing (3:16, 18 and 1 Thessalonians 5:23, 28). The differences are as striking: the warm personal memories of 1 Thessalonians 2-3 are missing here, and the teaching on the end has a different emphasis.

Three explanations are offered: Paul wrote twice to the same church within a short time, repeating himself as people do; Paul wrote this letter first (Wanamaker); or a later writer used 1 Thessalonians as his model (Wrede, Trilling, Menken). The authorship table above gives each view's arguments. 1 Thessalonians is being written on this site at the same time as this letter; the notes refer to its verses by number.

sections.h: The man of lawlessness in Christian history
sections.b: Paul never uses the word "antichrist"; that word is John's (1 John 2:18, 22; 4:3; 2 John 7). But from Irenaeus on, Christians joined Paul's man of lawlessness to Daniel's arrogant king and little horn, to Jesus' warning about the abomination of desolation (Matthew 24:15) and to Revelation's beast, and spoke of one Antichrist. The early church expected a single deceiver at the end (Irenaeus, Chrysostom). The Reformers identified him with the papacy (Smalcald Articles; Westminster Confession 25.6 in its 1646 form; Second London Baptist Confession 26.4). Modern futurists, including dispensationalists, expect a future world ruler; preterists look to the first century; idealists see a pattern of evil in every age. The Catholic Catechism (675) speaks of "the supreme religious deception" of the Antichrist without naming anyone. See the antichrist topic and the cards on chapter 2.

The Greek text is stable; a recent full study of the manuscripts (Edwards, 2020) found only five places where its own text differs from NA28. A few readings matter for the English: "the man of lawlessness" or the KJV's "man of sin" (2:3); "as firstfruits" or "from the beginning" (2:13), a single letter's difference on which the editions divide; "the Lord Jesus" or "the Lord" (2:8); and "they", "you" or "he received" (3:6). The Plain English Translation follows the SBL edition and NA28, except at 1:2, where it follows NA28 and the Tyndale House edition. Each variant is set out where it occurs, with the witnesses.

spec.title: Claude's theory: a letter that practices what it preaches about time
spec.body: This is my own observation. The letter's three problems share one root: the wrong sense of time. Those who thought the day had come (2:2) lived as if the future had already arrived; those who stopped working (3:6-12) lived as if ordinary time no longer mattered; and the persecuted (1:4-7) were tempted to think that because justice had not come yet, it never would. The letter answers each with the same move: not yet, but surely. Justice is coming, but at the revealing of the Lord Jesus; the end is coming, but after the rebellion; meanwhile, work quietly and eat your own bread. If this is right, the 'not yet' of chapter 2 and the 'keep working' of chapter 3 are one teaching, which supports the view (held by many commentators) that the idleness and the false claim about the day were connected.

prompts: The letter that seems to be from us

A small house church in Thessalonica at night: a dozen men and women, workers in plain tunics, crowd around an oil lamp while one of them holds up a papyrus letter, and others look at it in alarm; outside the window the walls of a Roman city and a distant harbor with ships. Sketched by hand onto old rolled parchment, mixing cave-painting ochre figures with soft modern watercolor; wobbling ink lines, torn edges, no hard rectangular frame.
The one who sits in the temple

A shadowy crowned figure seated on a throne inside the doorway of a great stone temple, his arms raised as if claiming worship, while far above him a thin bright line of light, like breath, comes down from the sky; at the edges, small figures turn away. Drawn in the style of an ancient manuscript illumination mixed with cave-drawing silhouettes; rough parchment texture; soft torn borders, no sharp frame.
The greeting in my own hand

Close view of a hand holding a reed pen, writing a few large Greek letters at the bottom of a papyrus sheet covered in smaller, neater handwriting by another scribe; an inkpot and a lamp beside it. Sketched onto a scroll in brown ink and ochre wash, cave-art marks mixed with modern line drawing; soft edges and a torn margin, no rectangle.
reading: Abraham J. Malherbe, The Letters to the Thessalonians (Anchor Bible 32B, 2000)
A full commentary on both letters that defends Paul's authorship of the second and answers Trilling's arguments.
Charles A. Wanamaker, The Epistles to the Thessalonians (New International Greek Testament Commentary, 1990)
A commentary on the Greek text that defends Paul's authorship and argues that 2 Thessalonians was written first.
Maarten J. J. Menken, 2 Thessalonians (New Testament Readings, 1994)
A short study that reads the letter as written by a follower of Paul, and explains why.
Wolfgang Trilling, Untersuchungen zum zweiten Thessalonicherbrief (1972)
The German study that made the case against Paul's authorship widely persuasive.
Grant G. Edwards, The Text and Transmission of 2 Thessalonians (PhD thesis, Birmingham, 2020)
A full study of the manuscripts, with a new critical text and a textual commentary.
John Chrysostom, Homilies on Second Thessalonians
Five sermons from the late fourth century; homily 4 gives the classic early reading of the restrainer as the Roman Empire.
